One approach to multicore scheduling is to reserve all scheduling decisions, I/O processing, and other system activities for a single processing core, called the master server. The other processes execute only user code. This asymmetric multiprocessing is simple because only one core accesses system data structures, reducing the need for data sharing. Though, this approach allows the master server to become a potential bottleneck for overall system performance. The standard approach for supporting multiprocessors is symmetric multiprocessing (SMP), where each processor is self-scheduling. Scheduling proceeds by having the scheduler for each processor examine the ready queue and select a thread to run. This provides two possible strategies for organizing the ready threads: All threads may be in a common ready queue. This creates possible race conditions if two processors select the same thread simultaneously. We could use some form of locking to protect the common ready queue, though, locking will be highly contended as all accesses to the ready queue will require lock ownership. Each processor may have its own private ready queue. This is the most common approach on SMP systems. Private ready queues may also lead to more efficient use of cache memory. Though, the main drawback of such an approach is load balancing; though, balancing algorithms exist to equalize the workloads among all processors. When processor accesses memory, it spends a significant amount of time waiting for that memory to become ready, such a situation is referred to as a memory stall. This occurs primarily because modern processors run at much faster speeds than memory. However, memory stalls can also occur as the result of a cache miss. Recent hardware designs have implemented multithreaded processor cores in which two or more hardware threads are assigned to each core. That way, if one hardware thread stalls as a result of a memory access, the core can switch to another thread. From an OS perspective, each hardware thread maintains its architectural state, such as its program counter (PC) and register set, and thus appears as a logical CPU that is available to run a software thread. This technique is known as chip multithreading (CMT). Intel processors use the term hyperthreading or simultaneous multithreading (SMT) to describe assigning multiple hardware threads to a single processing core. In general, there are two ways to multithread a processing core: Coarse-Grained: A thread executes on a core until a long-latency event such as a memory stall occurs. The core then switches to another thread. The cost of thread switching is high, since the instruction pipeline must be flushed before the other thread can begin executing. Fine-Grained: Switches between threads at a fine level of granularity, typically at the boundary of an instruction cycle. The architectural design of fine-grained systems include logic for thread switching. As a result, the cost of switching between threads is small. The hardware resources of the physical core (such as caches and pipelines) must be shared among its hardware threads; therefore, a processing core can execute only one thread at a time. A multithreaded, multicore processor requires two levels of scheduling: On one level are the scheduling decisions made by the OS as it chooses which software thread to run on each hardware thread (logical CPU). A second level of scheduling specifies how each core decides which hardware thread to run. On SMP systems, it is important to keep the workload balanced among all processors, a problem known as load balancing. Load balancing is typically necessary on systems where each processor has its own private ready queue. There are two general approaches to load balancing: Push Migration: A specific task periodically checks the load on each processor. If it finds an imbalance, it balances the load by pushing threads from overloaded to underloaded cores. Pull Migration: Occurs when an idle processor pulls a waiting task from a busy processor. Push and pull migration are often implemented in parallel on load-balancing systems. When a thread runs on a CPU, the most recently accessed data is going populate the cache for that processor. As a result, successive memory accesses by the thread are often satisfied by cache memory. This situation is known as a warm cache. If the thread migrates to another processor, say due to load balancing, the contents of cache memory must be invalidated for the first processor, and the contents of the cache of the second processor must be repopulated. Because of the high cost of invalidating and repopulating caches, most operating systems try to keep threads running on the same processor, a technique known as processor affinity. With a global ready queue, a thread may be selected for execution by any processor. With private, per-processor ready queues, on the other hand, a thread is always scheduled on the same processor and can therefore reap the benefits of a warm cache. Essentially, pre-processor ready queues implement processor affinity for free. When an OS has a policy of attempting to keep a process running on the same processor, but not guaranteeing that it will do so, the OS implements soft affinity. Hard affinity, on the other hand, allow a process to specify a subset of processors on which it can run. Many systems provide both soft and hard affinity. The architecture of main memory can also affect processor affinity issues. A non-uniform memory access (NUMA) architecture is a memory design used in multiprocessor systems, where the access time to memory varies depending on the location of the memory relative to a processor. Although a system interconnect allows all CPUs in a NUMA system to share one physical address space, a CPU has faster access to its local memory than to memory local to another CPU. If the OS's scheduler and memory-placement algorithms are NUMA-aware, then a thread that has been scheduled on a CPU can be allocated memory closest to where the CPU resides. Load balancing often counteracts the benefits of processor affinity. Furthermore, migrating a thread between processors may incur a penalty on NUMA systems, where a thread may be moved to a processor that requires longer memory access times. Therefore, there is a natural tension between load balancing and minimizing memory access times. Many mobile systems now include multicore architectures, though, each core may vary in terms of its clock speed and power management. Such systems are known as heterogeneous multiprocessing (HMP). The intention behind HMP is to mange power consumption by assigning tasks to certain cores based upon the specific demands of the task. For ARM processors, this architecture is known as big.LITTLE where high-performance big cores are combined with energy efficient LITTLE cores. A CPU scheduler can assign tasks that don't require high performance, but may need to run for longer periods, to little cores, thereby preserving battery charge. Furthermore, if the mobile device is in power-saving mode, energy-intensive big cores can be disabled entirely and the system can rely solely on energy-efficient little cores. CPU scheduling for real-time operating systems (RTOS) introduce special issues. Soft real-time systems provide no guarantee as to when a critical real-time process will be scheduled. They guarantee only that the process will be given priority over noncritical processes. In hard real-time systems, on the other hand, a task must be serviced by its deadline. Service after the deadline is the same as no service at all. Real-time systems are typically event-driven. Events may arise in software, such as when a timer expires, or in hardware, such as when a sensor detects an object. Event latency is the amount of time that elapses from when an even occurs to when it is serviced. Two types of latencies affect the performance of real-time systems: Interrupt Latency: The period of time from the arrival of an interrupt at the CPU to the start of the interrupt service routine (ISR). The interrupt latency includes the time it takes for the OS to finish the instruction it is currently executing, determine the type of the interrupt, save the state of the current process, and service the interrupt using the corresponding ISR. For hard real-time systems, interrupt latency must not simply be minimized, it must be bounded. Interrupt latency also includes the amount of time that interrupts may be disabled while kernel data structures are being updated. Hard real-time systems require that interrupts be disabled for only short periods of time. Dispatch Latency: The amount of time required for the scheduling dispatcher to stop one process and start another. The most effective technique for keeping dispatch latency low is to provide preemptive kernels. The most important factor of a RTOS is to respond immediately to real-time processes as soon as such a process requires the CPU. Therefore, the scheduler for a RTOS must support a priority-based algorithm with preemption. Though, such a scheduler only guarantees soft real-time functionality. Hard real-time systems must guarantee that real-time tasks will be serviced before their deadlines. Real-time processes are considered periodic. That is, they require the CPU at constant intervals. A process may have to announce its deadline requirements to the CPU scheduler. Then, using a technique called an admission-control algorithm, the scheduler does one of two things: it either admits the process, guaranteeing that it will complete on time, or it rejects the request as impossible to fulfill. The rate-monotonic scheduling algorithm schedules periodic tasks using a static priority policy with preemption. Upon entering the system, each periodic task is assigned a priority inversely based on its period. The shorter the period, the higher the priority, and vice versa. The reasoning behind this is to assign a higher priority to tasks that will need the CPU more often. Rate-monotonic scheduling also assumes that the processing time of a periodic process is the same for each CPU burst. Rate-monotonic scheduling is considered optimal in the sense that if a set of processes cannot be scheduled by this algorithm, it cannot be scheduled by any other algorithm that assigns static priorities. A drawback of rate-monotonic scheduling is that CPU utilization is bounded, and it is not always possible to maximize CPU resources fully. The worst-case CPU utilization for processes is: Earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling assigns priorities dynamically according to the process's deadline. The earlier the deadline, the higher the priority. Under this policy, when a process becomes runnable, it must announce its deadline to requirements to the OS. EDF scheduling does not require that processes be periodic, nor must a process require a constant amount of CPU time per CPU burst. EDF is theoretically optimal; theoretically, it can schedule processes so that each process can meet its deadline requirements and CPU utilization will be 100 percent. In practice, however, it is impossible to achieve 100 percent CPU utilization due to the overhead of context switching and interrupt handling. Proportional share schedulers allocate time shares among all applications. An application can receive shares, thus causing the application to be allocated of the total processor time. Proportional share schedulers must work in conjunction with an admission-control policy to guarantee that an application receives its allocated shares of time. An admission-control policy will admit a client requesting a particular number of shares only if sufficient shares are available. Since version 2.6, the Linux kernel uses a scheduler known as the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). Scheduling in Linux is based on scheduling classes. Each class is assigned a specific priority. By using different scheduling classes, the kernel can accommodate different scheduling algorithms based on the needs of the system and its processes. Standard Linux kernels implement two scheduling classes: a default scheduling class using the CFS scheduling algorithm, and a real-time scheduling class. The CFS scheduler assigns a proportion of CPU time to each task. This proportion is based on the nice value assigned to each task. Nice values range from -20 to 19, where a numerically lower nice value indicates a higher relative priority. The default nice value is 0. Tasks with high nice values are considered nice to the other tasks in the system because they lower their own relative priority. CFS doesn't use discrete values of time slices. Instead, it identifies a target latency, which is an interval of time during which each runnable task should run at least once. Proportions of CPU time are allocated from the value of the target latency. The targeted latency can increase if the number of active tasks in the system grows beyond a certain threshold. The CFS scheduler doesn't directly assign priorities. Rather, it records how long each task has run by maintaining the virtual runtime of each task using the per-task variable vruntime. The virtual runtime is associated with a decay factor based on the priority of a task: lower-priority tasks have higher rates of decay than higher-priority tasks. For tasks of normal priority (i.e., tasks with nice values of 0), virtual runtime is equivalent to actual runtime. For tasks with lower-priority, their vruntime will be higher than their physical runtime. For tasks with higher-priority, their vruntime will be lower than their physical runtime. The decide which task to run next, the scheduler simply selects the task with the smallest vruntime value. Additionally, a higher-priority task that becomes available to run can preempt a lower-priority task. Linux also implements real-time scheduling according to the POSIX standard. Any task scheduled with either the SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_RR real-time policy runs at a higher priority than normal tasks. Real-time tasks are assigned static priorities within the range of 0-99, and normal tasks are assigned priorities from 100-139. These two ranges map into a global priority scheme where numerically lower values indicate higher relative priorities. Normal tasks are assigned priorities based on their nice values. The CFS scheduler also supports load balancing, using a technique that is NUMA-aware and minimizes the migration of threads. CFS defines the load of each thread as a combination of the thread's priority and its average rate of CPU utilization. When wanting to select a CPU-scheduling algorithm for a particular system, we must first define the criteria to be used in selecting an algorithm. Criteria are often defined in terms of CPU utilization, response time, or throughput. Once the selection criteria have been defined, we want to evaluate the algorithms under consideration. Evaluation methods include: Deterministic Modeling: Analytic evaluation uses the given algorithm and the system workload to produce a formula or number to evaluate the performance of the algorithm for that workload. Deterministic modeling is one type of analytic evaluation. This method takes a particular predetermined workload and defines the performance of each algorithm for that workload. Deterministic modeling is simple and fast, though, it requires exact numbers for input, and its answers apply only to those cases. The main uses for deterministic evaluation are in describing algorithms and providing examples.
Queuing Models: On many systems, the processes that run vary from day to day. Though, we can determine the distribution of CPU and I/O bursts by either measuring or simply estimating. These result is a mathematical formula describing the probability of a particular CPU burst. It is common for the distribution to be exponential, and is typically described by its mean. Similarly, we can describe the arrival-time distribution; that is, the distribution of times when processes arrive in the system. From these two distributions it is possible to compute the average throughput, utilization, waiting time, and so on, for most algorithms. The computer system is described as a network of servers. Each server has a queue of waiting processes. The CPU is a server with its ready queue, as is the I/O subsystem with its device queues. Knowing arrival rates and service rates, we can compute utilization, waiting time, etc. This area of study is called queuing-network analysis. Let be the average long-term queue length, let be the average waiting time in the queue, and let be the average arrival rate for new processes in the queue. We expect during the time that a process waits, new processes will arrive in the queue. If the system is in a steady state, then the number of processes leaving the queue must be equal to the number of processes that arrive. Therefore: This equation is known as Little's formula, and is particularly useful because it is valid for any scheduling algorithm and arrival distribution. We can use Little's formula to compute one of the three variables if we know the other two. At the moment, the classes of algorithms and distributions that can be analyzed using queuing analysis are fairly limited. The mathematics of complicated algorithms and distributions can be difficult to work with. It is also generally necessary to make a number of independent assumptions that may not hold in real systems. Simulation: To get more accurate evaluations of scheduling algorithms, we can use simulations. Software data structures represent the major components of the system. The simulator has a variable representing a clock. As this variable increases, the simulator modifies the system state to reflect the activities of the devices, processes, and scheduler.
The data to drive the simulation can be generated in many ways. The most common method is to use a random number generator that is programmer to generate processes, CPU burst times, arrivals, departures, and so on, according to probability distributions. The distributions can be defined mathematically or empirically. If the distributions are to be defined empirically, actual measurements of the system under study must be taken. Distribution-driven simulation may be inaccurate, however, because of the relationships between successive events in the real system. A frequency distribution only indicates how many instances of a particular event occur; it gives no information regarding the order of their occurrence. To address this shortcoming, we can use trace files. We create a trace by monitoring the real system and recording the sequence of actual events. We then use this sequence to drive the simulation. Implementation: Even a simulation is of limited accuracy. The only complete way to evaluate a scheduling algorithm is to implement it in the actual system and monitor its performance. A cooperating process is one that can affect or be affected by other processes executing in the system. Cooperating processes can either directly share an address space, or be allowed to share data only through shared memory and message passing. Concurrent access to data may result in data inconsistency. A process can be interrupted at any point in its instruction stream, and the processing core may be assigned to execute instructions of another process. Furthermore, two instruction streams (representing two separate threads) can be executing in parallel across multiple cores. Such conditions can lead to problems such as: Race Conditions: Occur when multiple processes/threads access shared data simultaneously, resulting in unpredictable results if one thread writes data while the other is reading it. Careful synchronization is required to prevent such situations. Synchronization is commonly implemented using locks. A process that wants to write to a shared data resource must acquire this lock. Once the writing process obtains the lock, no other thread can access the shared data until the lock is released. Deadlocks: Occur when multiple threads are waiting indefinitely for a resource (typically a lock) held by another thread. Proper resource allocation strategies must be carried out to avoid deadlocks. Starvation: Occur when a process never gets a resource that it needs (such as a lock) to complete its execution because other processes are continuously prioritized over it. The producer-consumer problem described in Chapter 3 is a common problem used to demonstrate synchronization requirements for cooperating processes. We described how a bounded buffer can be used to enable processes to share memory. The bounded-buffer solution has a fixed-size buffer, which the producer stores data into, and the consumer reads data from. We could have a separate variable count, which stores the amount of data items currently in the buffer. If count == size(buffer) - 1, then the buffer must be full; if count == 0, then the buffer must be empty. Whenever the producer writes to the buffer, it can also increment the count variable. Conversely, the consumer can decrement count whenever it reads from the buffer. The problem with this solution is that the count variable can be incremented and decremented simultaneously by the producer and consumer threads, respectively. Furthermore, either the producer or the consumer can be interrupted/preempted in between the instruction that writes/reads the buffer, and the instruction that increments/decrements the count variable. This can lead to incorrect and unpredictable results when executing the program concurrently. A situation like this, where both processes can access and manipulate the same data simultaneously, and the outcome depends on the particular order in which the accesses take place, is an example of a race condition. To remedy this, we need to ensure that one process can manipulate the shared data at a time. Additionally, while one process is manipulating the data, no other process should be able to read the data until the writing process is finished. Each cooperating process has a particular segment (or segments) of code which may access or update shared data. Such a segment of code is referred to as that process's critical section. The critical-section problem involves ensuring that no two processes can be in their critical section at the same time. We must design and implement a protocol that enables processes to synchronize their activities so they can cooperatively share data. Each process must seek permission to enter its critical section; the section of code implementing this request is known as the entry section. The critical section may be followed by an exit section, with the remaining code being the remainder section. A solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy the following requirements: Mutual Exclusion: If process is executing in its critical section, then no other process can be executing in their critical section. Progress: If no process is executing in its critical section and some processes wish to enter their critical sections, then only those processes that are not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding which will enter its critical section next, and this selection cannot be postponed indefinitely. Bounded Waiting: There exists a bound on the number of times that other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter its critical section before that request is granted. The critical-section problem can be solved simply in a single-core system by preventing interrupts from occurring while a shared variable is being modified. Unfortunately, this solution is not feasible in a multiprocessor system since disabling interrupts on a multiprocessor can be time consuming, since the message must be passed to all processors. Two general approaches exist for handling critical sections in operating systems:
Preemptive Kernels: Allows a process to be preempted while it is running in kernel mode. Such kernels are especially difficult to design for SMP architectures, since in these environments it is possible for two kernel-mode processes to run simultaneously on different cores. Though, preemptive kernels may be more responsive, since there is less risk that a kernel-mode process will run for a long period of time. Furthermore, a preemptive kernel is more suitable for real-time programming, as it will allow a real-time process to preempt a process currently running in the kernel. Nonpreemptive Kernels: Does not allow processes in kernel to be preempted. Such a kernel is free from race conditions on kernel data structures. Software-based solutions to the critical-section problem, such as Peterson's solution, are not guaranteed to work on modern computer architectures because of the way such architectures reorder machine instructions. Though, there exist hardware instructions that provide support for solving the critical-section problem. These primitive operations can be used directly as synchronization mechanisms, or they can be used to form the foundation of higher-level synchronization tools. How a computer determines what memory guarantees it will provide to an application is known as its memory model. Generally, memory models fall into one of two categories: Strongly Ordered: A memory modification on one processor (core) is immediately visible to all other processors. Weakly Ordered: Memory modifications on one processor may not be visible to all other processors immediately. Memory models vary by processor type, so kernel developers cannot make any assumptions regarding the visibility of modifications to memory on a shared-memory multiprocessor. To address this problem, computer architectures provide instructions that can force any changes in memory to be propagated to all other processors. Such instructions are known as memory barriers/fences. When a memory barrier instruction is performed, the system ensures that all loads and stores are completed before any subsequent load or store operations are performed. Therefore, even if instructions were reordered, the memory barrier ensures that the store operations are completed in memory and visible to other processors before future memory operations. Many modern architectures provide special instructions that enable a programmer to test and modify the content of a word, or to swap the contents of two words atomically, that is, in one uninterruptible operation. Such instructions may be referred to as the test_and_set and compare_and_swap instructions, respectively. Such instructions can be used to implement mutual exclusion: The test_and_set instruction be used to implement mutual exclusion by having a binary lock variable (lock) initialized to 0. The test_and_set instruction can be used change the value of the lock conditionally and atomically. If two cores were to attempt the change the value of lock simultaneously, since the instruction is atomic, one will certainly execute before the other. When a process exits its critical section, it sets lock back to 0, which enables another process to enter its critical section. The compare_and_swap (CAS) instruction can also be used to implement mutual exclusion. A global variable (lock) is initialized to 0, the first process that invokes compare_and_swap will set the lock to 1. It will then enter its critical section because the original value of lock was equal to its expected value of 0. Subsequent calls to compare_and_swap will fail because lock is not equal to the expected value of 0. When a process exits its critical section, it sets lock back to 0, which enables another process to enter its critical section. Although these algorithms satisfy the mutual exclusion requirement, they do not satisfy the bounded-waiting requirement. Typically, the CAS instruction is not used directly to provide mutual exclusion. Rather, it is used as a basic building block for construction other synchronization tools, such as atomic variables. Atomic variables provide atomic operations on basic data types such as integers or Booleans. Most systems that support atomic variables provide special atomic data types as well as functions for accessing and manipulating such types. These functions are often implemented using CAS operations. 123 A. Silberschatz, Operating System Concepts. S.L.: John Wiley, 2021.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
